section_1.title: Prerequisites & Intuition (1 min)
section_1.content: Define a discrete signal as a sequence of numbers (e.g., pixel intensities). Explain the concept of a 'sliding window' or 'kernel' as a tool to transform a target pixel based on its neighbors.
section_1.example: Imagine a 3x3 grid of pixels representing a tiny part of a cat's face; we want to calculate the average brightness to smooth the image.

section_2.title: The Mechanism of Convolution (1.5 min)
section_2.content: Define discrete convolution mathematically as the weighted sum of input elements within a kernel. Use visual animation showing a kernel flipping, sliding across an input matrix, and performing element-wise multiplication followed by summation.
section_2.example: Visualizing a 'Blurring Kernel' (all values 1/9) sliding over an image, replacing the center pixel with the average of its 8 neighbors.

section_3.title: The Power of Kernels (1.5 min)
section_3.content: Demonstrate how changing kernel weights produces different effects. Explain that convolution is essentially a filter that extracts specific patterns from signals or data structures.
section_3.example: Contrast two kernels: a 'Blur' kernel (averaging) versus an 'Edge Detection' kernel (Sobel filter) that highlights the silhouette of a bird against the sky.

section_4.title: Real-world Applications (1 min)
section_4.content: Summarize how convolutions are the foundation of modern computer vision, specifically in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Conclude with how they process layers of visual data to recognize complex objects.
section_4.example: A smartphone camera app: The device automatically applies a convolution filter to sharpen your selfie or detect faces by recognizing the high-contrast edges of eyes and mouths.
